site_article.hero_alt: Vercel's announcement card for v0, its AI app builder.

paragraphs.text: If you want to know how to use Vercel v0 for free, here is the short answer: sign in at v0.app, describe the app you want in plain words, check the live preview, fix details with more prompts or in Design Mode, and press Publish to put it online. Vercel describes v0 as an AI agent that helps anyone create real code and full stack apps, and its FAQ says no coding experience is required.

Under the hood, v0 writes a normal web project. The FAQ lists the stack as Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui, and you can write your prompt in any language. Because the result is real code, you can keep working on it yourself, sync it to GitHub or deploy it somewhere other than Vercel.
How to use Vercel v0: your first app

paragraphs.title: 1. Sign in at v0.app
paragraphs.text: Go to v0.app and sign in. If you already have a Vercel account, you can use it; the FAQ says you do not need a separate account.

paragraphs.title: 2. Start a chat and describe the app
paragraphs.text: Start a new chat or create a project, then describe your idea in normal sentences. Vercel's own quickstart examples are as simple as a todo app with add, edit and delete, or a contact form that sends emails. You can also start from a screenshot, a mockup or a Figma design, which the FAQ lists as ways to begin.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 1: A first app that is small enough to finish
paragraphs.text: Build a simple habit tracker. I can add a habit with a name, tick it off for today, and see a 7 day streak for each habit. Use a clean, light design with one accent color. Keep everything on one page and store the data in the browser for now.

paragraphs.title: 3. Review the preview and iterate
paragraphs.text: v0 shows the generated app in a preview. Click through it like a user would, then send follow up prompts for what is wrong. One change per message works better than a list of ten, because you can see exactly what each prompt did.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 2: Fix one thing at a time
paragraphs.text: On mobile, the habit list overflows the screen. Make the list stack in one column under 640 px wide and keep the add button visible at the bottom. Do not change anything else.

paragraphs.title: 4. Edit in the Code tab when you know what to change
paragraphs.text: The preview toolbar has a Code tab. The quickstart says you can select lines in the gutter and add a comment as context, then send your next prompt, so v0 knows exactly which lines you mean. The FAQ adds that a full code editor in the style of VS Code is built in.

paragraphs.title: 5. Use Design Mode for visual tweaks
paragraphs.text: Open the Design tab in the same toolbar, select an element on the page and change its style with the visual controls or by typing an instruction. Click Apply and the edit is written into the source code as a new version of the chat.
Use Design Mode for colors, spacing and text sizes, and save your prompts for behavior and layout. Every chat prompt uses credits, and Design Mode lets you make those changes directly on the element.
Connect data, GitHub and a domain

paragraphs.title: 6. Add a database or payments
paragraphs.text: Open the project menu, then Settings, then Integrations. The quickstart lists databases from Neon, Supabase, Upstash for Redis and Blob storage, AI model providers including Grok, fal, Deep Infra and Vercel AI Gateway, and Stripe for payments. Secret keys go under Settings, then Environment Variables.

paragraphs.title: 7. Sync with GitHub (optional)
paragraphs.text: Under Settings, then GitHub, you can connect a repository. According to the FAQ, v0 then works on its own branch, commits every code change, can open pull requests and never pushes straight to your main branch. The sync works both ways, so changes you make locally come back into v0.

paragraphs.title: 8. Publish it
paragraphs.text: Use the Publish control in the chat header. The first time, v0 may ask you to confirm a Vercel project name, then lets you pick visibility and a domain. Your app gets an address ending in vercel.app by default, and you can connect your own domain later under Settings, then Domains. After that, Publish Changes updates the same live address.
Vercel v0 plans and free limits

The v0 FAQ lists five plans: Free, Premium at $20 a month, Plus at $30 per user a month, Business at $100 per user a month, and Enterprise with custom terms. It also says Premium is being retired and is no longer open to new users. Team collaboration on shared projects needs Plus, Business or Enterprise.

The FAQ does not spell out how much the free plan includes. Two reviews from early 2026 by other software companies do: NxCode and Taskade both say the free plan comes with $5 of credits a month, and NxCode adds a limit of 7 messages a day plus up to 200 projects. Both say v0 moved to pricing based on tokens in February 2026, so a large request costs more than a small one. NxCode lists three model tiers, v0 Mini, v0 Pro and v0 Max, with Max the most expensive per token.

Those numbers come from reviews, not from Vercel's docs, and they can change. Check your own usage page in v0 before a big build, and pick the cheapest model that does the job when you are making small edits.
What v0 is not good at

v0 is strongest at the part most people get stuck on: a good looking, working first version of a web app. It is tied closely to Next.js and Vercel. Both reviews call that ecosystem lock in a weakness, and NxCode notes there is no native mobile app output. Credits can also go fast: NxCode warns that heavy use of the top model can burn through the free $5 in a single session, and Taskade says heavy users report the same.

Vercel's own FAQ is plain about limits too. v0 needs an internet connection, the generated code may be incomplete or contain bugs, and you are responsible for checking that it fits your use. The full experience with previews, environment variables and deployments assumes your GitHub repository is connected to a Vercel project, although you can export the code and host it elsewhere.

The practical way to use the free plan is to treat it as a sketchbook. Build one small app end to end, publish it, and learn where v0 needs precise prompts. If you hit the daily or monthly limit before the app works, that is the moment to judge whether a paid plan is worth it for you.
